title: Lecture 3 from zero: insertion sort, loop invariants, and what O, Ω and Θ are for
summary: One idea at a time: insertion sort with cards, then the code next to plain English; what a loop invariant is and why it proves the sort works; counting steps on the best and worst input; what Big-O, Omega and Theta are each for and how to think about them; and exactly why O(log n) and O(n log n) are so different.
sourceNote: A slower retelling of Lecture 3 (Loop Invariants, Insertion Sort) and the parts of Lectures 4 and 5 it leads into (asymptotic notation, binary search, merge sort), matching the facts in the Lecture 2 to 3 and Lecture 4 to 5 chapters. The insertion sort example [5, 2, 4, 6, 1, 3] is the textbook's (CLRS). Every count, curve and table is computed by the script that builds this chapter.

blocks.md: Every algorithm in this course gets asked the same **two questions**: **Is it correct?** (does it give the right answer for every possible input, not just the ones you tried?) and **How fast is it?** (how does the work grow when the input gets bigger?). Lecture 3 answers both for one small algorithm, **insertion sort**. Loop invariants answer the first question. Big-O, Omega and Theta answer the second.

blocks.md: **Why it matters** Lecture 3 is the vocabulary for the rest of the course. Every later algorithm (merge sort, heaps, quicksort, BSTs, AVL) gets the same treatment: show it works, then say its O, Ω or Θ. If these two ideas click now, the next ten lectures are new examples of the same thing.

sections.heading: Insertion sort, with cards (no code yet)

blocks.md: Picture sorting a hand of playing cards as you're dealt them. You keep the cards **in your hand sorted** at all times. Each new card, you slide it left past every card bigger than it, and drop it in the gap. When the deck runs out, your whole hand is sorted.

blocks.body: Keep a **sorted left part** of the list. Take the next item (the **key**), slide it left past every bigger item, and drop it in the gap. Repeat until the sorted part is the whole list.
The item currently being placed. In the card picture, the new card in your other hand.
Everything to the **left** of the key: a[0..j−1]. It's always sorted, even though it isn't in its final place yet (smaller items can still arrive later and push things right).

blocks.title: Insertion sort on [5, 2, 4, 6, 1, 3], card by card

frames.caption: Your hand starts as the first card, 5. One card is already sorted.
Pick up 2: slide it left past 5. Your hand is now [2, 5].
Pick up 4: slide it left past 5. Your hand is now [2, 4, 5].
Pick up 6: it's already bigger than everything in your hand, so it stays put. Your hand is now [2, 4, 5, 6].
Pick up 1: slide it left past 6, 5, 4, 2. Your hand is now [1, 2, 4, 5, 6].
Pick up 3: slide it left past 6, 5, 4. Your hand is now [1, 2, 3, 4, 5, 6].
No cards left on the table. The whole hand is sorted: [1, 2, 3, 4, 5, 6].

blocks.prompt: In the middle of sorting [5, 2, 4, 6, 1, 3], the left part is [2, 4, 5, 6] and the key is 1. Where does 1 end up after this pass?
blocks.answer: At the very front: 1 is smaller than all four, so it slides past 6, 5, 4 and 2. The left part becomes **[1, 2, 4, 5, 6]**.

blocks.md: **How to read any loop:** find the variable that moves (here j, then i), say out loud what it points at, and say what the loop body does to that spot. 'j picks the next card; i walks left while the cards are bigger; each step slides one card right.' If you can say that sentence, you understand the code.

sections.heading: Loop invariants: a promise the loop keeps

blocks.md: **The problem.** You can test insertion sort on 10 arrays and it works. That proves nothing about the 11th. There are infinitely many inputs, so 'I tried it' is never a proof. We need a way to show it's right for **every** input.

blocks.body: A sentence about the loop's variables that is **true every time the loop checks its condition**: before the first pass, after every pass, and when it finally stops. It describes the progress made so far.
At the start of each pass of the for loop with index j: **a[0..j−1] is sorted** (and holds the same items that were there at the start).

blocks.md: **The bookmark picture.** Imagine a bookmark at position j. The promise is: 'everything left of my bookmark is sorted'. The loop's whole job is to move the bookmark right **without ever breaking the promise**. When the bookmark reaches the end, the promise covers everything.

rows: it's true before the loop starts
j = 1: a[0..0] is one item, and one item is always sorted
if it's true before a pass, it's still true after
the pass slides the key into the right spot in a sorted part, so a[0..j] is sorted
when the loop stops, invariant + stop condition give the answer
the loop stops at j = n, so a[0..n−1], the whole array, is sorted
blocks.title: The three parts, side by side
Watch the promise hold at every check

frames.caption: Initialization. Before the loop starts, j = 1. The invariant says a[0..0] is sorted. One card is always sorted, so it's true before we've done anything.
Maintenance. This pass inserted 2 into the sorted part. Back at the loop check with j = 2: is a[0..1] sorted? Yes. Still true, one card bigger.
Maintenance. This pass inserted 4 into the sorted part. Back at the loop check with j = 3: is a[0..2] sorted? Yes. Still true, one card bigger.
Maintenance. This pass inserted 6 into the sorted part. Back at the loop check with j = 4: is a[0..3] sorted? Yes. Still true, one card bigger.
Maintenance. This pass inserted 1 into the sorted part. Back at the loop check with j = 5: is a[0..4] sorted? Yes. Still true, one card bigger.
Termination. j = 6, so the loop stops. Plug j = 6 into the invariant: a[0..5] is sorted. That's the whole array, which is exactly the goal.

blocks.title: The four sentences to write on the exam (fill in the blanks for any loop)
blocks.body:
Invariant: at the start of each iteration, ____ (what's true about the part done so far).
Initialization: before the first iteration, ____ is true because ____.
Maintenance: if ____ holds before an iteration, the body ____, so it still holds after.
Termination: the loop stops when ____; then the invariant says ____, which is what we wanted.

rows: for i = 0 to n − 1: total += a[i]
insert a[j] into the sorted part
adding a[i] extends the sum by one
i = n: total = sum of everything
blocks.title: Same recipe, two loops

blocks.body: Writing the invariant about the **whole** array ('the array is sorted'). That's false in the middle of the loop. The invariant is always about the **part done so far**: a[0..j−1].

sections.heading: Counting steps: best case and worst case

blocks.md: Now the second question: how fast? We **count steps**, not seconds (seconds depend on the computer). For insertion sort, the step that matters is the **shift**: sliding a card right. How many shifts depends on what order the cards arrive in.

blocks.title: Sorted vs reversed, n = 5: count the shifts

frames.caption: Sorted input, n = 5. Count how many times an item slides right.
j = 1: the key 2 slides past 0 items. Already in place: one comparison and done.
j = 2: the key 3 slides past 0 items. Already in place: one comparison and done.
j = 3: the key 4 slides past 0 items. Already in place: one comparison and done.
j = 4: the key 5 slides past 0 items. Already in place: one comparison and done.
Sorted: 0 shifts in total. Best case: about n steps in all (just the comparisons): Ω(n).
Reversed input, n = 5. Count how many times an item slides right.
j = 1: the key 4 slides past 1 item.
j = 2: the key 3 slides past 2 items.
j = 3: the key 2 slides past 3 items.
j = 4: the key 1 slides past 4 items.
Reversed: 10 shifts in total. Worst case: 1 + 2 + 3 + 4 = 10 = n(n−1)/2: O(n²).

blocks.title: The gap explodes as n grows

blocks.md: Look at the last row: 1,000 items take about **1,000** steps when sorted but about **500,000** when reversed. Same algorithm, same n. So 'how fast is insertion sort?' has no single answer, and that's exactly why we need three different symbols.

sections.heading: O, Ω and Θ: what each one is for

blocks.md: **The point of all three:** we want to describe how the work **grows** as n grows, ignoring details that don't matter (the computer's speed, constant factors like 3n vs 5n, small terms like +10). Each symbol answers a slightly different question.

rows: no single Θ overall (n vs n²); worst case is Θ(n²)
blocks.title: The three symbols

blocks.md: **How to think about them:** O is a promise about the **worst** that can happen ('it won't be slower than this'). Ω is a promise about the **best** that can happen ('it can't be faster than this'). Θ is when both promises have the **same shape**, so you know the growth exactly. Poon uses O for the worst case and Ω for the best case.
blocks.label: think

blocks.caption: Θ(n²) as a picture: past n₀, the real step count stays between 3n² and 5n². Hover each line.

blocks.body: **f(n) = O(g(n))** if there are constants c > 0 and n₀ with f(n) ≤ c·g(n) for every n ≥ n₀. **f(n) = Ω(g(n))** if f(n) ≥ c·g(n) for every n ≥ n₀. **f(n) = Θ(g(n))** if both hold (with possibly different c's).

a ceiling can be too high; we always give the tightest one
even sorted input needs a comparison per item
on sorted input it's about n, so n² isn't a floor
merge sort is Θ(n log n)
best and worst are both n log n
you must touch all n items, never more
blocks.title: Check yourself: true or false?

blocks.body: Thinking O means 'worst case' by definition. O is just a ceiling on a function. It's the **worst-case running time** that we usually bound with O, which is why the two get said together.

sections.heading: O(log n) vs O(n log n): the two you'll mix up

blocks.md: These two look alike and are **completely different**. The 'log n' part means the same thing in both: **how many times you can cut n in half** before reaching 1. The difference is **how much work you do each time you halve**.

blocks.body: The number of halvings from n down to 1. 8 → 4 → 2 → 1 is **3** halvings, so log₂ 8 = 3. 1,000,000 needs only about **20**. That's why log n is so small.

rows: do **all n items** at **every** level of halving
**binary search**: look at the middle, throw away half
**merge sort**: split everything in half, merge all of it back
one loop that halves what's left
halving recursion, with an O(n) merge at each level

blocks.caption: Same 16 items, same 4 levels of halving. Binary search keeps one half (green path); merge sort keeps both and touches all 16 on every merge level.

blocks.title: O(log n): binary search throws half away each look

frames.caption: Find 23. The list is sorted. low and high mark the part that could still hold 23: right now, all 16 items.
Look 1: mid = (0 + 15) / 2 = 7. a[7] = 45, which is bigger than 23.
So 23 can only be LEFT of index 7. high = mid − 1 = 6. Half the candidates are gone in one comparison.
Look 2: mid = (0 + 6) / 2 = 3. a[3] = 12, which is smaller than 23.
So 23 can only be RIGHT of index 3. low = mid + 1 = 4. Half the candidates are gone in one comparison.
Look 3: mid = (4 + 6) / 2 = 5. a[5] = 23. Found it, after 3 looks. A left-to-right scan would have needed 6.

blocks.title: O(n log n): merge sort does n work on every level

frames.caption: log₂ 8 = 3 halvings turn 8 items into 8 pieces of 1. A piece of 1 is already sorted (the base case). No work yet.
frames.note: levels of merging so far: 0 · steps so far: 0

frames.caption: Merge level: 4 merges, each of 2 pieces of 1, make pieces of 2. Every one of the 8 items gets copied once: 8 steps on this level.
frames.note: levels of merging so far: 1 · steps so far: 8

frames.caption: Merge level: 2 merges, each of 2 pieces of 2, make pieces of 4. Every one of the 8 items gets copied once: 8 steps on this level.
frames.note: levels of merging so far: 2 · steps so far: 16

frames.caption: Merge level: 1 merges, each of 2 pieces of 4, make pieces of 8. Every one of the 8 items gets copied once: 8 steps on this level.
frames.note: levels of merging so far: 3 · steps so far: 24

frames.caption: 3 merge levels × 8 items per level = 24 steps = n · log₂ n. That's where n log n comes from: n work, repeated log n times.

blocks.title: Binary search vs merge sort, as code
blocks.body:
# O(log n): ONE loop, and it halves what's left each time
while lo <= hi:
    mid = (lo + hi) // 2
    if a[mid] == x: return mid
    if a[mid] < x: lo = mid + 1   # throw away the left half
    else: hi = mid - 1            # throw away the right half

# O(n log n): halve EVERYTHING, then merge ALL of it back
def merge_sort(a):
    if len(a) <= 1: return a
    m = len(a) // 2
    return merge(merge_sort(a[:m]), merge_sort(a[m:]))   # merge is O(n)
blocks.answer: log n vs n log n

blocks.caption: All four shapes on one chart. log n hugs the bottom; n log n is just above n; n² leaves the chart almost at once.

blocks.md: **The one sentence to remember:** log n = 'one path down the halvings'; n log n = 'every item, on every level of halving'. If the algorithm **throws away** half, it's log n. If it **keeps and processes** both halves, it's n log n.
blocks.label: think

blocks.body: Writing merge sort as O(log n) because 'it halves'. Halving gives you the **number of levels** (log n). You still have to count the **work per level**: merge sort merges all n items on each one.

blocks.md: **Go deeper:** both algorithms are animated step by step in the Lecture 4 to 5 chapter.
